opus-5.5.text:
I think what makes both of them interesting is that they made a very clear bet on data, and specifically on *how* to get real-world manipulation data at scale, rather than starting from the robot hardware or from a pure simulation story.

With Generalist, the thing that stands out to me is that they're really treating robotics as a scaling problem in the same spirit as language models. The founding team comes from a background of thinking about foundation models for robots, and their message has been fairly consistent: if you can collect enough diverse, real physical interaction data, you start to see scaling behavior, where bigger models and more data give you predictably better dexterity and generalization. That's a strong claim in robotics, because for a long time our field was stuck in this regime of small datasets, one task, one lab setup. So they're distinctive in being very model-centric and very empirical about scaling: they want to show the curves, not just the demos.

Sunday is a bit different in flavor. They're much more full-stack and product-oriented. They're thinking about the home, about an actual robot that lives in your house and does chores, and they've designed the data collection around that. The idea of using a wearable, glove-like device so people can do tasks naturally with their hands, and then that data transfers to the robot because the robot's end effector matches the device, is a very elegant co-design between hardware and learning. It sidesteps a lot of the pain of teleoperation, which is slow and expensive and hard to scale. And it lets you collect data in real homes, which are messy and diverse in a way labs never are.

So if I had to put it simply: Generalist is pushing hardest on the question "does robot learning scale like other foundation models?", and Sunday is pushing on "can you co-design the hardware, the data pipeline, and the product so that scaling actually becomes affordable in the real world?" Both of them come from people who did a lot of the foundational research on imitation learning and diffusion-style policies, so they understand where the bottlenecks actually are. And I think that's the common thread: neither of them believes the bottleneck is a clever algorithm anymore. They believe it's data, and the infrastructure to get that data. That's a fairly mature view, and I think it's why people in the field take both of them seriously.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think what makes both of them interesting is that they've each made a very deliberate bet on where the bottleneck in robotics actually is, and the bets are almost mirror images of each other.

Generalist is fundamentally a data-and-model company that happens to be in robotics. Their thesis is that the thing holding embodied AI back isn't hardware, it's that we've never had a dataset of physical interaction anywhere close to the scale of internet text. So they've gone all in on collecting enormous volumes of real-world manipulation data, far more than most labs would consider reasonable, and training foundation models on top of it. The hardware is almost secondary; they want to be the layer that any robot can run on. That's a very "scaling laws" worldview applied to the physical world, and it takes a lot of conviction, because collecting that data is slow and expensive in a way text scraping never was.

Sunday Robotics is coming at it from the opposite direction. They started from the question of what it would actually take to put a robot in a normal home and have it be useful, and that forced them to think about the whole product, not just the policy. The home is the hardest environment there is: cluttered, unstructured, every house is different, and the tolerance for failure is low because it's someone's living space. What I find clever about their approach is how they're attacking the data problem through the product itself. If you design the hardware and the data collection around each other, so that teaching the robot feels natural to a person rather than like running a lab, you can get data that's actually representative of homes, not of a warehouse mockup of a home.

So you have one company saying "solve the general intelligence problem and the applications will follow," and another saying "pick the hardest real application, solve it end to end, and the generality will come from the diversity of real homes." Both are rejecting the older robotics playbook of carefully engineering one task at a time with hand-tuned perception and planning.

What they share, and what I think separates them from a lot of the field, is that they're treating robotics as a learning problem rather than a controls problem, and they're honest about how much data that requires. A lot of startups talk about foundation models for robots and then quietly rely on teleoperation demos in a single lab. These two have actually built their companies around the unglamorous question of where the data comes from. In the end, I suspect that's what will decide who wins this space.

astra-6.text:
I’d look at them through two questions: how broadly can the robot learn, and how reliably can it do useful work? Those are related, but they’re not the same thing. A system can look very general in a demo and still need a lot of support in practice.

For Generalist AI and Sunday Robotics, I’d want to understand how each connects learning to deployment. Does experience on one task help with the next? Can the robot recover when something goes wrong? How much human intervention does it need?

I don’t have enough detail here to make a confident comparison between the two. But that’s where I’d look for a meaningful distinction: whether they can turn broader capabilities into dependable work, and whether deployment makes the system better over time.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d be careful about making a company-specific comparison without knowing more about their approaches. For me, the key question is where each team believes the bottleneck is: building a more general robot intelligence, or making the whole system reliable enough to do useful work in a particular setting.

Those are different bets. I’d judge distinctiveness by how well the robot handles unfamiliar situations, how much human intervention it needs, and how quickly the team can turn real-world experience into improvements. That’s what I’d want to understand about Generalist AI and Sunday Robotics before saying what truly sets either one apart.
